item.research_question: How does increasing Nb content in Al0.5Ti3Zr0.5NbxMo0.2 high-entropy alloys affect lattice structure, corrosion behavior, and the formation mechanism of the passivation film in 3.5% NaCl solution?
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc melting; samples prepared as plate-like alloys (3 mm thick, 0.5 mm width) and polished to 80 μm thickness; constant potential polarization at 1 VSCE and 4 VSCE for 40 min; dynamic potential polarization from -1 to 10 VSCE at 1 mV/s
item.test_conditions: 3.5% NaCl solution at room temperature; electrochemical tests (polarization curves, constant potential); XRD (Cu Kα, 40 kV, 20°–80°); SEM/TEM/EDS; XPS with Ar+ sputtering at 2.5, 10, and 20 nm depths
key_findings: The alloys exhibit a single-phase BCC structure with space group Im-3m; lattice constant increases slightly with rising Nb content.
Increasing Nb content reduces the {011} crystal plane spacing from 2.295 Å (x=0.5) to 2.282 Å (x=1), correlating with improved corrosion resistance.
The alloy with x=0.5 shows the highest self-corrosion current density (1.11 × 10⁻⁶ A/cm²) and lowest corrosion potential (-0.5787 VSCE).
The breakdown potential reaches 8.68 VSCE, indicating a wide and stable passivation zone superior to Ni, Zr, and Fe-based alloys.
Nb concentration in the passivation film is reduced by half compared to the substrate, while Ti and Al concentrations increase significantly.
The passivation film is ~1 μm thick (observed by SEM) and ~11 nm thick (observed by TEM cross-section), composed primarily of high-valent oxides (Ti⁴⁺, Nb⁵⁺, Zr⁴⁺, Al³⁺, Mo⁶⁺).
TEM analysis reveals the film contains nanocrystals (~10 nm) of TiO₂ (rutile), Nb₂O₅, and Al₂O₃, with an amorphous component.
Corrosion is preferential at {011} crystal planes, where the dissolution rate is faster than at {002} and {112} planes.
item.mechanism: Nb, having a large atomic radius and strong oxygenophilicity, induces uphill diffusion of smaller Ti/Al atoms and downhill diffusion of O. This leads to the formation of a layered passivation film where low-valent oxides form first and react with inward-diffusing O to create stable high-valent oxides (Al₂O₃/TiO₂). Additionally, increasing Nb reduces {011} crystal plane spacing, limiting corrosive fluid channels and slowing dissolution.
item.limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study, though it notes that the formation process of passivation films and their internal structure were seldom involved in prior studies, implying a gap this work fills rather than a limitation of this work itself.
item.future_work: The authors state the work provides a basis for designing chemically robust alloys for extreme environments but do not explicitly propose specific future experiments.
quotes: Nb improves the corrosion resistance of high-entropy alloys in two main ways.
Increasing Nb content reduced the {011} crystalline plane spacing, enhancing the corrosion resistance of Al0.5Ti3Zr0.5NbMo0.2.
Nb, which has a large atomic radius and strong oxygenophilicity, interacts with each metal element, contributing to the uphill diffusion of Al/Ti and the downhill diffusion of O.
